sourceHtml:
Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself.

In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land:

  1. A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces.
  2. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint.
  3. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update.

We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it

SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights.

The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary:

Check What it guards Why it misses SDC
ECC memory Catches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result.
Xid errors (NVRM) GPU driver/hardware faults The GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs.
DCGM deep health check hardware faults Misses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job.
NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksums transport Verify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly.
Checkpoint checksums storage round-trip A poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine.

The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself.

Solution overview

The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features:

Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas.

Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup.

Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards.

Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window.

Figure 1: A SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster with three p5 nodes running training pods and SDC checks. Node 1 raises an alarm for rank 13, and the proposed steps cordon the node, check GPU metrics, replace it, and restart training

It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different:

Layer Source What it adds Catches truly silent SDC?
1. Non-finite gradient check Your training script Names a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf Only faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow
2. Ring replay audit Your training script Every GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprints Yes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps
3. Weight fingerprint comparison Your training script Names a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the update Yes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights
4. Localization Your training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node names Maps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node name n/a: it localizes
5. DCGM correlation HyperPod observability add-on The suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarm It confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node.
6. Deep health check StartClusterHealthCheck (DCGM L4) An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect node It catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof
7. Repeat-offender history A query you build over retained alarms and telemetry Nodes that alarm repeatedly Partly: it surfaces nodes worth checking early

Layers 1–3 are the only layers that detect silent SDC, and they live in your training code. Layer 4 turns their alarm into an instance ID, and the HyperPod layers corroborate the alarm and close the loop.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, with at least three GPU nodes. The ring audit needs three different nodes for every comparison it settles, and the weight comparison needs three copies of each weight to name the odd one out. See Orchestrating SageMaker HyperPod clusters with Amazon EKS.
  • A PyTorch DDP training job in which every replica runs its own optimizer step, with a data pipeline that can rebuild any rank’s micro-batch for a given step, such as a seeded sampler.
  • Checkpoints on shared storage, Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Replacing a node destroys its root and secondary volumes, including anything on local NVMe.
  • The SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on for the correlation step. Turn on advanced DCGM metrics if you want ECC, NVLink, and throttling counters.
  • Access to the cluster through kubectl, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for sagemaker:StartClusterHealthCheck and sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes. See Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

Step 1: Detect with three checks in your training loop

Data parallelism trains several copies of the model, called replicas, at the same time. Each replica trains on a different slice of the batch. After each backward pass, an all-reduce averages the replicas’ gradients, and every replica applies that same average in optimizer.step(). Here’s one weight across three replicas, with a learning rate of 0.1:

replica 0 replica 1 replica 2
weight at start 0.500 0.500 0.500 same
local gradient 0.20 0.40 0.30 different (different data)
averaged gradient 0.30 0.30 0.30 same, after the all-reduce
weight after step 0.470 0.470 0.470 same

Local gradients differ, because each replica sees different data. And after the optimizer step, the weights must be identical, bit for bit.

Where a fault lands decides which check can see it. If replica 1 computes a local gradient of 4.00 instead of 0.40, the all-reduce spreads that error to every replica: all three apply the same wrong update, and their weights still match. Only replica 1’s local gradient looked different, and only before the all-reduce. If instead replica 1 corrupts a weight during or after the optimizer step, its weights no longer match the others. There’s one exception: a NaN or Inf in one replica’s weights reaches every replica through the next all-reduce, and after that the replicas agree again. A fault inside the all-reduce itself, such as a GPU that adds a partial sum wrong, also reaches every replica identically.

So compute-path faults must be caught before the optimizer step, while the bad gradient can still be discarded, and faults in the update or in stored weights after it. Finite wrong values need recompute: comparing gradient norms across replicas catches only NaN and Inf (see Why not compare local gradient norms?). That gives three checks on every DP rank, in a fixed order within each training step:

  1. Non-finite gradient check – Before the all-reduce, flag any rank whose local gradient is NaN or Inf. This catches values that blow up in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step they happen, and names the GPU. After the all-reduce, check the reduced gradient for NaN or Inf too, before the update.
  2. Ring replay audit – On audit steps, before the optimizer step, every rank recomputes the micro-batch of a rank on another node. It compares the loss bit for bit and, with deterministic kernels, every parameter’s gradient fingerprint. This catches finite wrong values in the compute path.
  3. Weight fingerprint comparison – After the optimizer step, every N steps and before every checkpoint, compare every replica’s weight fingerprints. This catches faults in the optimizer step and in stored weights.

The code in this step is for PyTorch DDP. For tensor, pipeline, or context parallelism, see Beyond DDP.

Order of execution

Figure 2: Flowchart of one training step. Check 1 (NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce) and check 2 (ring replay, on audit steps) run before the optimizer step and stop the step if they fire. Check 3 (weight fingerprints) runs after it and blocks the checkpoint

Why not compare local gradient norms?

A natural first design, and the one we started with, flags a rank whose local gradient norm is more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median of that step. We recorded every rank’s local gradient norm on every step of the three fault-free runs on 4 instances (22,800 steps, see Fault-free runs) on 32 H100s training a 953-million-parameter model, and the test doesn’t work:

  • The healthy spread is too wide – Each rank sees different data, so healthy local norms already reached 224 MADs in the first 800 steps, and 1,240 MADs over all healthy steps.
  • A quiet threshold sees nothing finite – At k = 336, 1.5 times the highest score in the first 800 healthy steps, it raised 11 false alarms in the remaining 22,000 healthy steps. And no finite fault came close: the faulty rank’s score never exceeded 6.9, even with one activation multiplied by 10,000.

Compare by fingerprint

Checks 2 and 3 compare tensors across GPUs. Sending whole tensors would cost too much, so each tensor is reduced to a fingerprint: two 64-bit sums of its raw bit patterns, one plain and one weighted by position. Any change to one or two elements of a tensor changes the fingerprint, for tensors with fewer than 2³² elements of up to 4 bytes each. That covers every weight fault we injected. Larger changes could, in principle, cancel out, so equal fingerprints are strong evidence of equal tensors, not proof. The position-weighted sum matters: in our tests, a swap of two weight values and a compensating change to two values left the plain sum unchanged, and only the weighted sum caught them.

_INT_VIEW = {1: torch.uint8, 2: torch.int16, 4: torch.int32, 8: torch.int64}

@torch.no_grad()
def fingerprints(tensors, chunk=1 << 24):
    # ... picks the device and allocates out: one row of two int64 per tensor
    for k, t in enumerate(tensors):
        if t is None:
            continue
        bits = t.detach().contiguous().view(-1).view(_INT_VIEW[t.element_size()])
        for i in range(0, bits.numel(), chunk):  # chunked to bound temporary memory
            b = bits[i:i + chunk].to(torch.int64)
            pos = torch.arange(i + 1, i + 1 + b.numel(), dtype=torch.int64, device=dev)
            out[k, 0] += b.sum()
            out[k, 1] += (b * pos).sum()
    return out

Check 1: NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce

A DDP communication hook records each rank’s local gradient before it’s averaged. It stores the squared norm of every gradient bucket and, on deterministic audit steps, the fingerprints of every parameter’s gradient (used by check 2). Then it passes the bucket to PyTorch’s standard all-reduce.

After backward, nonfinite_ranks gathers one scalar from every rank and returns the ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf. The first rank flagged is the faulty one. If the step were applied, the NaN would reach every rank on the next step.

def local_stats_hook(stats, bucket):
    stats.sq.append(bucket.buffer().float().pow(2).sum())
    if stats.record_fingerprints:  # per parameter, before allreduce_hook divides in place
        rows = [stats.row[p.data_ptr()] for p in bucket.parameters()]
        stats.fp[rows] = fingerprints(bucket.gradients())
    return allreduce_hook(stats.dp_group, bucket)

def attach(ddp_model, dp_group):
    stats = LocalStats(dp_group, list(ddp_model.module.parameters()))
    ddp_model.register_comm_hook(state=stats, hook=local_stats_hook)
    return stats

def nonfinite_ranks(stats):
    """After backward: global ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf."""
    local = torch.stack(stats.sq).sum().sqrt().reshape(1)
    n = dist.get_world_size(stats.dp_group)
    gathered = [torch.empty_like(local) for _ in range(n)]
    dist.all_gather(gathered, local, group=stats.dp_group)
    bad = ~torch.isfinite(torch.cat(gathered).cpu())
    return [dist.get_global_rank(stats.dp_group, r) for r in bad.nonzero().flatten().tolist()]

train() also checks the gradient after the all-reduce. A NaN or Inf produced inside the reduction reaches every replica the same way, so the copies still match and check 3 passes them. Without this check, the NaN becomes NaN weights on every replica, and a checkpoint due on that step is saved with them and tagged as passing. clip_grad_norm_ already computes the norm of the reduced gradient, so the check adds only one one-element all-reduce per step. A finite error in the reduction still passes every check.

If you train with fp16 and a gradient scaler, exclude the overflow steps the scaler already skips. bf16 doesn’t have them.

Check 2: Ring replay, before the optimizer step

Every replica holds the same weights until optimizer.step(). So, between the backward pass and the optimizer step, any rank can recompute any other rank’s micro-batch, and with deterministic kernels it must get the same bits.

On an audit step, every rank r recomputes the micro-batch of rank r + 8: 8 positions ahead, which is one node away on p5 instances. It uses the unwrapped module, so nothing is all-reduced, and it restores the gradients, the module’s buffers, and the random-number state afterwards. A replay blocks the job no matter how many ranks do one, so auditing every rank costs the same wall-clock time as auditing one.

Each rank then appears in two comparisons: its own micro-batch, replayed by a peer, and the micro-batch it replayed for someone else.

  • Both comparisons mismatch: That rank computed wrong in both, so it’s the culprit.
  • Only one mismatches: Either side could be wrong. confirm settles it in place: the GPU eight positions after the target, on a third node, and the target itself replay the target’s micro-batch again. That also tells a persistent fault, which the target reproduces, from a transient one, which it doesn’t.
def ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats, local_loss, offset, with_grads):
    # ... g is the DP group, n its size, and me this rank's position in it
    target = dist.get_global_rank(g, (me + offset) % n)
    replay = _replay(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch(step, target), with_grads)
    # ... v = [this rank's own loss bits and gradient fingerprints, its replay of target]
    dist.all_gather_into_tensor(out, v, group=g)
    table = out.view(n, 2, -1).cpu()  # per DP rank: [own result, its replay of its target]
    pairs = [(dist.get_global_rank(g, (r + offset) % n), dist.get_global_rank(g, r))
             for r in range(n) if not torch.equal(table[(r + offset) % n, 0], table[r, 1])]
    return pairs, table

def localize(pairs):
    hits = Counter(r for p in pairs for r in p)
    culprits = sorted(r for r, c in hits.items() if c >= 2)
    ambiguous = [p for p in pairs if not set(p) & set(culprits)]
    return culprits, ambiguous

def confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, pair, table, stats, offset, with_grads):
    # ... the third GPU (target + offset) and the target replay the target's micro-batch again
    third_r, self_r = v.cpu()
    orig, peer = table[ti, 0], table[ri, 1]
    if torch.equal(third_r, orig):
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": replayer, "kind": "replayer computed wrong"}
    if torch.equal(third_r, peer):
        kind = ("persistent" if torch.equal(self_r, orig) else
                "transient" if torch.equal(self_r, third_r) else "unclear")
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": target, "kind": kind}
    return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": None, "kind": "unattributable"}

The confirmation is only independent if the three GPUs are on three different nodes. check_topology verifies that for every pair before training starts, from each pod’s NODE_NAME, and raises an error otherwise.

Choose the audit mode:

  • Default kernels: Compare the loss only. This needs a forward pass whose loss is bitwise reproducible, which held in our tests: healthy replays matched the original loss bit for bit. Gradients can’t be compared this way, because attention’s default backward pass isn’t deterministic. This mode catches forward-pass faults that change the loss.
  • Deterministic kernels (deterministic_audits=True): The whole audit step runs with deterministic algorithms and the math attention kernel. Gradient fingerprints then match too, so the audit also catches backward-only faults. An op with no deterministic implementation raises an error instead of producing a false alarm. On our model, a deterministic audit step cost 2.4 times a default one.

Never replay a suspect’s work on the suspect alone. A GPU with a persistent defect can reproduce its own wrong answer.

Check 3: Weight fingerprints, after the optimizer step

After optimizer.step(), every replica’s weights must be identical, so there’s no tolerance to tune. Each rank fingerprints every weight tensor and gathers everyone’s fingerprints.

A rank is named only when its copy of a tensor differs from a strict majority, more than half of the copies. With two copies, or a split with no strict majority, the comparison reports a disagreement without naming any rank.

def find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group):
    local = fingerprints(params).flatten()
    # ... all-gathers every rank's fingerprints into table: [dp_size, num_tensors, 2]
    differs = (table != table[0]).any(dim=2).any(dim=0)
    if not differs.any():
        return {"diverged": False, "suspects": []}
    suspects = set()
    for k in differs.nonzero().flatten().tolist():
        copies = [tuple(row) for row in table[:, k].tolist()]
        value, count = Counter(copies).most_common(1)[0]
        if 2 * count <= n:
            return {"diverged": True, "suspects": None}  # no strict majority for tensor k
        suspects.update(r for r, c in enumerate(copies) if c != value)
    return {"diverged": True,
            "suspects": sorted(dist.get_global_rank(dp_group, r) for r in suspects)}

Run it every N steps and on every checkpoint step. It’s the only check that runs after the update, so it’s the only one that can stop a checkpoint from being written out of a corrupted copy. In our tests, a weight corrupted right after one update was caught at the next checkpoint step, and the save didn’t happen. Without the forced check, the save went ahead from the corrupted copy, and the ring audit noticed only at the next audit, five steps later.

It costs 31.1 ms per check on a 953-million-parameter model: 2 percent of a step when it runs every 10 steps.

Put the checks in the training loop

train runs each step in the order of Figure 2 and stops at the first alarm. It decides whether a step is an audit step before the forward pass, because a deterministic comparison needs the original computation to be deterministic too. When check 1 or 2 fires, it zeros the gradients and returns without clipping or applying the update, so the bad gradient never reaches the weights or the optimizer state, and the exact state is still there for confirmation. After clipping, it checks whether the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf, and if it is, returns before the update. It saves a checkpoint only if nothing fired.

def train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, save_checkpoint,
          sched, start_step=0):
    # ... setup, including check_topology(dp_group, sched.peer_offset)
    for step, batch in enumerate(batches, start_step):
        audit = step % sched.audit_every == 0  # 0. decide first
        det = audit and sched.deterministic_audits
        # ... resets the hook's per-step state
        with deterministic() if det else nullcontext():
            loss = compute_loss(ddp_model, batch)  # 1. forward, backward
            loss.backward()
        nonfinite = nonfinite_ranks(stats)  # 2. non-finite check
        pairs, table = [], None
        if audit or nonfinite:  # 3. ring replay
            pairs, table = ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats,
                                      loss, sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det)
        if nonfinite or pairs:  # 4. gate
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            culprits, ambiguous = localize(pairs)
            verdicts = [confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, p, table, stats,
                                sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det) for p in ambiguous]
            return {"step": step, "check": "compute", "nonfinite": nonfinite,
                    "mismatched_pairs": pairs, "culprits": culprits, "verdicts": verdicts,
                    "suspect_window": _window(last_audit, step, start_step),
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        if audit:
            last_audit = step
        grad_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, sched.max_grad_norm)
        bad = (~torch.isfinite(grad_norm)).to(torch.int32).reshape(1)  # reduced gradient
        dist.all_reduce(bad, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=dp_group)
        if bad.item():
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            return {"step": step, "check": "reduced gradient", "suspect_window": [step, step],
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        ckpt = step % sched.ckpt_every == 0
        if step % sched.check_every == 0 or (ckpt and sched.check_on_checkpoint):
            wc = find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group)  # 5. weight check
            if wc["diverged"]:
                return {"step": step, "check": "weights", "suspects": wc["suspects"],
                        "suspect_window": _window(last_weights, step, start_step),
                        "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
            last_weights = step
        if ckpt:  # 6. checkpoint
            save_checkpoint(step, tags={"last_audit_pass": last_audit,
                                        "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights})
    return None

The alarm’s suspect_window is the range of steps since the last pass of the check that fired. A fault that was active on every step since it started began inside it. An intermittent fault can be older, and a fault that no check sees can be in any checkpoint, so treat the tags as a record that the checks passed at that step, not as proof that the saved state is clean.

A training script calls it like this:

# ... imports, and the model, optimizer, and dataset setup
import sdc_order as S

stats = S.attach(ddp_model, dp_group)  # registers the comm hook, once
sched = S.Schedule(audit_every=10, deterministic_audits=True, check_every=10,
                   ckpt_every=100, peer_offset=8)  # 8 = GPUs per node

def compute_loss(model, batch):  # used for training AND replay
    x, y = batch
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits = model(x)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.float().flatten(0, 1), y.flatten())

def rebuild_batch(step, rank):  # exactly the micro-batch `rank` trained on
    return dataset.micro_batch(step, rank)

# ... batches(start) yields this rank's micro-batches and sets the learning rate
alarm = S.train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches(start), compute_loss, rebuild_batch,
                save_checkpoint, sched, start_step=start)
if alarm is not None:
    report_sdc(alarm)  # metric + log line; Step 2 maps the rank to a node
    sys.exit(3)

The replay depends on these:

  • Exact micro-batches: rebuild_batch(step, rank) must return exactly the micro-batch that rank trained on, for example from a seeded sampler.
  • Same loss function: compute_loss must be the same function in training and in replay, including autocast, and any randomness inside it, such as dropout, must be seeded per step and rank.
  • No collectives or output-affecting state in the model: The confirmation replay runs on only two ranks, the target and the third GPU, so a model that calls a collective inside its forward or backward pass (SyncBatchNorm, for example) hangs on an ambiguous alarm. A buffer that the forward pass both reads and updates makes a healthy replay differ.
  • Deterministic setup: Set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 before the training process starts, and make sure every op in the model has a deterministic implementation.
  • Peer offset: Number DP ranks node by node, so that peer_offset equal to the GPUs per node puts every replayer on another node. check_topology refuses a layout where it doesn’t.
  • Untested here: Unused parameters, gradient accumulation, BatchNorm, and forward hooks with side effects. With unused parameters, set deterministic_audits=False, which compares the loss only.

audit_every is the main cost-versus-robustness setting:

  • Detection delay: A persistent finite fault is caught within audit_every steps if it also occurs in the kernels the audit runs. Deterministic audits run deterministic kernels and the math attention kernel, so a fault confined to the default kernels used on the other steps is never audited.
  • Corrupted updates: Up to audit_every − 1 corrupted updates can be applied before the audit catches it. They’re inside the alarm’s suspect_window.
  • One-time faults: A finite fault on a single non-audit step that doesn’t recur isn’t caught at all.

Make ckpt_every a multiple of both audit_every and check_every, so every checkpoint step is audited before its update and fingerprinted after it.

We measured the average step time end to end, over 1,000 consecutive steps per schedule, on the 953M model and 32 H100s. Every schedule with the checks also runs the weight check every 10 steps:

Schedule Average step time Over plain DDP
Plain DDP, no checks 157.4 ms —
Checks, no audits 169.0 ms +7.4%
Deterministic audits every 10 steps 211.9 ms +34.7%
Default-kernel audits every 10 steps 177.0 ms +12.5%
Deterministic audits every 100 steps 173.3 ms +10.1%
Default-kernel audits every 100 steps 169.3 ms +7.6%

About 7 percentage points of each schedule’s cost don’t depend on audits: the gradient hook and the two NaN/Inf checks on every step, and the weight check every 10 steps. A reasonable starting point for production is deterministic audits every 100 steps, which cost 10 percent here. They still catch a persistent fault within 100 steps, including a backward-only one, at the price of up to 99 corrupted updates to roll back. Audit every 10 steps when you need faster detection, for example during a burn-in on new capacity or while you watch a suspect node. Measure the cost on your own model: deterministic attention uses the math kernel, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

In the fault-free runs, 15,320 audit steps and 3,080 weight checks raised no alarm, which bounds the false-alarm rate at about 1 in 5,100 audit steps (95 percent confidence).

Step 2: Localize the suspect rank to a node

A rank is a logical ID. To act on it, you need the instance and the physical GPU. On HyperPod EKS, the Kubernetes node name is the instance ID with a hyperpod- prefix. Pass it to your pod with the Kubernetes downward API:

env:
- name: NODE_NAME  # on HyperPod EKS, spec.nodeName is "hyperpod-<instance-id>"
  valueFrom:
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: spec.nodeName

At job start, log a table that maps every rank to its node, instance, and GPU UUID:

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

node = os.environ["NODE_NAME"]  # "hyperpod-i-0123456789abcdef0"
instance_id = node.removeprefix("hyperpod-")  # "i-0123456789abcdef0", what the Replace API takes
gpu_uuid = "GPU-" + str(torch.cuda.get_device_properties(torch.cuda.current_device()).uuid)
info = {"rank": dist.get_rank(), "node": node,
        "instance_id": instance_id, "gpu_uuid": gpu_uuid}
table = [None] * dist.get_world_size()
dist.all_gather_object(table, info)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    print("rank_map", table)  # log at every job start

If a job is already running without the downward API, you can map a pod to its node from outside with kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'.

Step 3: Contain the damage and check the GPU metrics

When an alarm fires, stop the job first. Then stop new work from landing on the suspect node by cordoning the node while you investigate:

kubectl cordon <node-name>  # marks the node unschedulable; existing pods keep running

Then open the GPU health dashboard in the SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on, filter to the suspect node and GPU, and look at the time the alarm fired. A rise in correctable ECC errors, PCIe replays, throttling, or temperature on that GPU raises confidence that the hardware is at fault. A clean panel doesn’t clear the node: pure SDC often leaves no trace in hardware telemetry.

Step 4: Confirm, then replace the node

With the Step 1 checks running, an alarm already names a suspect GPU. When you see a symptom without an alarm, such as a loss spike, or want to rule out software before you replace anything, start with the cheap explanations. Most loss spikes aren’t SDC, and chasing SDC on a data bug wastes days:

Loss anomaly / suspected corruption
- Reproduces with the same seed on DIFFERENT nodes? -> deterministic bug, not SDC
- Goes away, or follows one node, when you move the job? -> strong SDC candidate
- DP replicas that must be bitwise identical disagree? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's step replayed on another node gives different bits? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's pre-all-reduce gradient is NaN or Inf? -> SDC candidate (use the first step it fired)
- Fleet-wide and gradual? -> likely recipe or optimizer
- Started at a data, config, or library change? -> usually software, but not proof

The test that separates SDC from software is whether the problem follows the hardware:

  • A reproducible failure doesn’t rule out SDC – Meta pinned a failing workload to one core and got the same wrong answer every time for specific inputs.
  • Neither does a failure that starts at a software change – Google traced one incident to a correct library update that began using rarely used instructions on defective cores.
  • Don’t expect the global loss to point anywhere – A forward fault first changes the faulty rank’s own loss, and the all-reduce then spreads its gradient to every replica. Per-rank checks and replays give you the locality.

Decide what the alarm means

Alarm Meaning Suggested action
check == "weights", suspects == [r] Rank r’s copy differs from a strict majority after the update Keep r’s node cordoned. Replace it after review
check == "weights", suspects is None Copies disagree, but no strict majority Ambiguous: keep the nodes involved cordoned. Check DCGM and run deep health checks
culprits == [r] Both of r’s ring comparisons mismatched. This assumes at most one faulty GPU among the GPUs that replay each other (the GPUs with the same local index). With two, a healthy GPU can be named Keep cordoned. Replace after review, or after the fault repeats
Verdict persistent The target reproduced its own wrong answer, and a third GPU agreed with the replayer Keep cordoned. Replace after review
Verdict transient The target’s retry came out right and agreed with the third GPU. An intermittent fault can look the same Keep cordoned until an audit with the node as the target, or a deep health check, passes. Replace it if it happens again
Verdict replayer computed wrong The replaying GPU, not the target, was wrong Treat the replayer as the suspect, and confirm again
nonfinite set, no mismatched pairs NaN or Inf in a backward pass that the loss doesn’t show, or a gradient norm too large for float32 (above about 1.8 × 10¹⁹) Ambiguous: audit with the suspect as the target, or check DCGM and run a deep health check
check == "reduced gradient" The gradient was NaN or Inf after the all-reduce, although every rank’s local gradient was finite. No rank is named Ambiguous: keep the job stopped, check DCGM and run deep health checks on every node in the job, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the alarm step
Verdict unattributable or unclear The three GPUs don’t line up Ambiguous: check DCGM and run deep health checks on the nodes involved

In production, keep a human approval on every replacement until you have evidence of the checks’ precision on your own workload. Synthetic tests like ours don’t establish it.

Confirm an ambiguous alarm

A deep health check is the main tool for ambiguous alarms. Its stress tests catch faults that the hardware reports, and subtle data-dependent faults often pass. To run one on the suspect instance group:

aws sagemaker start-cluster-health-check \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --deep-health-check-configurations '[{"InstanceGroupName":"<instance-group>","InstanceIds":["i-0123456789abcdef0"],"DeepHealthChecks":["InstanceStress"]}]'

Replace the node

When you’re ready to replace the node, you have two options. Both trigger the same SageMaker HyperPod recovery process, described in Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

If automatic node recovery is turned on, you can label the node and let SageMaker HyperPod replace it, which is convenient for automation:

kubectl label node <node-name> \
    sagemaker.amazonaws.com/node-health-status=UnschedulablePendingReplacement --overwrite

To use the API instead, run:

aws sagemaker batch-replace-cluster-nodes --cluster-name <cluster-name> --node-ids <instance-id>

On clusters that use Karpenter for autoscaling, BatchReplaceClusterNodes terminates the node but creates a replacement only if pending pods need one. After the replacement joins, the training job restarts through the SageMaker HyperPod training operator or the job’s restart policy, and your training script resumes from the newest checkpoint saved before the alarm’s suspect_window starts. Call find_divergent_ranks right after loading it, before the first step. Replacement destroys the node’s root and secondary volumes, so keep checkpoints on shared storage.

Automating the workflow

The manual steps are for understanding. In production, wrap them in a small controller that runs in your own cluster and account:

  1. Trigger: The training job reports the alarm as a Kubernetes event, a small custom resource (for example SDCReport{rank, job, step, check}), or an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on metrics such as sdc_nonfinite_grad, sdc_replay_mismatch, and sdc_divergent_tensors.
  2. Resolve: The controller maps rank → pod → node through the Kubernetes API, then node → instance ID by stripping the hyperpod- prefix.
  3. Contain: It cordons the node.
  4. Decide: It applies the table in Step 4. The ring audit has already confirmed ambiguous pairs in place, so the alarm carries the verdicts. For an ambiguous result, it runs one node-scoped deep health check.
  5. Recover: For a replacement, it asks a human to approve, then calls BatchReplaceClusterNodes, or sets the node-health label if automatic node recovery is turned on. Then it relies on the training operator and your checkpoint reload, and records every step in CloudWatch.

Build it as a lightweight Kubernetes operator, or as an Amazon EventBridge rule on the CloudWatch alarm that invokes an AWS Lambda function.

Use case: Testing the checks on SageMaker HyperPod

We ran the tests twice on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, using 4 and then 3 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs each, and PyTorch 2.9.0 (CUDA 13.0) from the AWS Deep Learning Containers training image. The model was a 953-million-parameter Llama-style decoder with 16 layers, a hidden size of 2,048, 16 attention heads, a 32,000-token vocabulary, and 2,048-token sequences. Each GPU processed 2 sequences per step (131,072 tokens per step on 32 GPUs), with fp32 weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and bf16 autocast for compute. We trained with AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ after a 100-step linear warm-up, with betas of (0.9, 0.95), weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The data was synthetic: a copy task with Zipf-distributed tokens whose first half repeats, seeded per rank and step so that any micro-batch can be rebuilt.

Fault scenarios

Faults were injected in one layer, the MLP down-projection of the eighth of 16 decoder blocks, on a chosen rank and step:

  • Forward faults change the layer’s output but keep its gradient path, like a wrong multiply in the forward pass.
  • Backward-only faults change the gradient of the layer’s input or weight.
  • Weight faults change one GPU’s copy of the stored weight right after the optimizer step: a bit flip, a swap of two values, or a compensating change to two values.
  • A persistent fault recurs in everything the faulty GPU computes, including the replays it runs for other ranks. A transient fault fires once.

Every scenario restarts from a snapshot taken after 400 warm-up steps, and step numbers count from it. Unless noted, audits ran every 10 steps with deterministic kernels, weight checks every 10 steps, and a checkpoint every 20. The table shows the 4-instance results. On 3 instances, every scenario raised the same alarm, at the same step, from the same check, naming the same ranks. Only the peer ranks changed.

Fault-free runs

To measure false alarms, we trained without faults on both cluster sizes, with three schedules each. Every schedule ran the weight check every 10 steps and saved no checkpoints, and each run’s length was fixed in minutes, so the two schedules that audit every step contribute most of the audit steps:

Instances Audits Minutes Steps Audit steps Weight checks Alarms
4 Deterministic, every step 45 4,600 4,600 460 0
4 Default kernels, every step 22.5 5,400 5,400 540 0
4 Deterministic, every 10 steps 45 12,800 1,280 1,280 0
3 Deterministic, every step 15 1,600 1,600 160 0
3 Default kernels, every step 7.5 2,000 2,000 200 0
3 Deterministic, every 10 steps 15 4,400 440 440 0
Total 150 30,800 15,320 3,080 0

With 0 alarms in 15,320 audit steps, the rule of three puts a 95 percent upper bound of 3 / 15,320, about 1 in 5,100, on the false-alarm rate per audit step. The NaN/Inf checks didn’t fire on any fault-free step either. The gradient-norm analysis in Why not compare local gradient norms? uses the 4-instance runs only.

Beyond DDP

The weight comparison isn’t limited to DDP. find_divergent_ranks takes any data-parallel group, so it also applies to tensor, pipeline, and context parallelism, HSDP, and mixture of experts, which are all layouts that keep independent copies of each weight. It can’t help under ZeRO-1 or full FSDP sharding, where each shard’s update is computed on only one rank. We tested the checks and the training loop in this post only with DDP.

To use it in another layout, call find_divergent_ranks with the group that holds copies of the same shard. With only two copies, it can detect a disagreement but can’t name the faulty copy.

If you’d rather have the service check your nodes for you, SageMaker HyperPod also offers the MultiNodeTraining deep health check. It runs a short, fixed distributed training job across a batch of GPU nodes, with no code changes, and replaces nodes whose training loss turns NaN or Inf, diverges, or doesn’t finish in time. Select it alongside InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity when you create an instance group, or run it on demand with StartClusterHealthCheck. It complements the checks in this post: use it to screen new and replacement nodes before your job lands on them, and the in-job checks to catch wrong values in your own training that never become NaN or Inf. For details, visit SageMaker HyperPod Deep Health Checks.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete what you created for testing. If you created a HyperPod cluster, delete it with aws sagemaker delete-cluster --cluster-name <cluster-name>. That removes only the HyperPod resources. Delete the EKS cluster, its add-ons, and any Amazon FSx volumes separately, after the HyperPod cluster. See Deleting a SageMaker HyperPod cluster.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to detect silent data corruption in data-parallel training and how to hand a suspect node to SageMaker HyperPod for replacement. Three checks cover the three places a fault can land: a NaN/Inf check on each rank’s gradient and on the reduced gradient, a ring replay that compares every GPU’s work with a GPU on another node, and a weight fingerprint comparison after the update. Run the first two before the optimizer step, don’t apply a step that failed a check, and compare weights before every checkpoint. Node names on SageMaker HyperPod EKS clusters turn the suspect rank into an instance ID. Then quarantine the node, roll back to a checkpoint from before the suspect window, and let the node-health label or the Replace API complete the recovery.

To get started, review the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency features for Amazon EKS, and try the companion repository. To go deeper, see deep health checks and the observability add-on.

静默数据损坏（SDC）是指 GPU 等硬件返回一个错误但看似合理的数值，却不报错。在分布式训练中，这个错误数值可能流入每个副本的梯度和权重。损失值可能连续数小时看起来都正常，等团队发现无法解释的发散或模型能力下降时，算力已经消耗掉了。这在大规模训练中确实会发生：Meta 在使用最多 16K 块 H100 GPU 进行Llama 3 405B 预训练的 54 天内，将 419 次意外作业中断中的 6 次归因于静默数据损坏，而这还只是那些导致作业中断并被追溯到 SDC 的情况。

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod 已经能够替换报告故障的节点：运行状况监控代理监视 GPU 错误，深度运行状况检查对节点进行压力测试，自动节点恢复则替换故障硬件。SDC 会绕过所有这些功能，因为硬件从不报告任何异常。检测必须由训练作业自身完成。

本文在 PyTorch DistributedDataParallel（DDP）训练循环中加入三项检查来检测 SDC。检查触发时，我们将可疑 rank 映射到其所在节点，遏制损坏扩散，并让 SageMaker HyperPod 替换该节点。每项检查覆盖故障可能发生的不同位置：

  1. 非有限梯度检查会在 GPU 的前向或反向传播发生 NaN、Inf 和溢出的当步捕获它们，同时捕获梯度 all-reduce 引入的 NaN 或 Inf。
  2. 环形重放审计捕获有限的错误值。在审计步，每块 GPU 都会重新计算另一个节点上的一个微批次，逐位比较损失值，并通过指纹比较梯度。
  3. 权重指纹比较通过比较更新后每个副本的权重，捕获优化器步骤中以及已存储权重中的损坏。

我们在一个包含 4 个 ml.p5.48xlarge 实例（32 块 NVIDIA H100 GPU）的 SageMaker HyperPod 集群上，通过软件注入故障来测试这些检查，并在三个实例上重复了每项测试，这是这些检查所需的最少实例数。本方案的完整代码可在配套 GitHub 仓库中获取。

静默数据损坏如何发生，以及常规检查为何会漏检

SDC 源于制造缺陷（未被供应商筛查发现的临界晶体管）以及特定计算单元的芯片老化，最常见于张量核心中的乘加通道，而这恰恰是模型训练会高强度使用的硬件。这种处于临界状态的电路大多数时候计算正确，只有在高温、电压骤降或特定操作数模式等压力条件下才会出错。由于算术逻辑路径没有 ECC 或奇偶校验保护（内存则有），错误结果，比如本应为 4.0000 却得到 4.0001，永远不会被标记，并会经过激活值和梯度流入每个副本的权重。

它如此难以捕获，是因为SDC 发生在计算路径中，而你现有的每项完整性检查守护的都是其他边界：

检查 保护对象 为何漏检 SDC
ECC 内存 捕获内存中的位翻转，而非错误的数学运算。张量核心的计算结果没有 ECC 保护。
Xid 错误（NVRM） GPU 驱动程序/硬件故障 GPU 检测到故障时会报告 Xid。SDC 按定义不会报告任何错误，因此 /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA 日志中不会出现任何记录。
DCGM 深度运行状况检查 硬件故障 无法发现需要你的工作负载中的操作数、热状态或时序才能触发的缺陷。它在空闲节点上运行，独立于你的作业。
NVLink / PCIe / EFA 校验和 传输 验证收到的字节是否与发送的一致，而非它们是否计算正确。
检查点校验和 存储写入与读回 已被污染但内部一致的检查点仍能通过校验和检查。

捕获 SDC 的方法是检查计算结果本身。

方案概述

整个流程有四个步骤。前两步由训练作业完成，后两步使用 Kubernetes 和 SageMaker HyperPod 的功能：

步骤 1。检测：训练循环中的三项检查通过比较数据并行副本，指出可疑 GPU。

步骤 2。定位：在由 Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service（Amazon EKS）编排的 SageMaker HyperPod 集群中，Kubernetes 节点名称包含实例 ID，因此将可疑 rank 映射到节点只需进行一次查找。

步骤 3。遏制并关联分析：停止作业，将节点标记为不可调度，并在 SageMaker HyperPod 可观测性仪表板中查看其 GPU 指标。

步骤 4。确认并恢复：在告警含义不明确时进行确认，审核后替换节点，并从可疑时间窗口之前保存的检查点恢复。

图 1：一个包含三个 p5 节点的 SageMaker HyperPod EKS 集群，运行着训练 Pod 和 SDC 检查。节点 1 针对 rank 13 发出告警，建议步骤包括将节点标记为不可调度、检查 GPU 指标、替换节点以及重启训练

将整个流程视为分层结构有助于理解，每一层提供不同的能力：

层 来源 提供的能力 能捕获真正静默的 SDC 吗？
1. 非有限梯度检查 你的训练脚本 在 all-reduce 之前指出本地梯度为 NaN 或 Inf 的 GPU，并在归约后的梯度为 NaN 或 Inf 时停止当前训练步 仅限于变成 NaN、Inf 或溢出的故障
2. 环形重放审计 你的训练脚本 每块 GPU 重新计算另一个节点的微批次，并比较损失值的位模式和梯度指纹 可以，在审计步捕获改变损失值或梯度的有限计算路径故障
3. 权重指纹比较 你的训练脚本 在更新后指出权重与严格多数副本不同的副本 可以，针对单个副本中的优化器步骤故障和已存储权重故障。无法发现计算路径故障，也不适用于分片权重
4. 定位 你的训练脚本，使用 SageMaker HyperPod 节点名称 从 Kubernetes 节点名称中获取实例 ID，将可疑 rank 映射到该实例 ID 不适用：它负责定位
5. DCGM 关联分析 HyperPod 可观测性附加组件 可疑 GPU 在告警前后的 DCGM 指标 仅在故障也体现在硬件计数器中时才能确认。遥测数据正常并不能排除节点故障。
6. 深度运行状况检查 StartClusterHealthCheck（DCGM L4） 对可疑节点进行按需硬件诊断 捕获其自身测试模式能触发的硬件缺陷。用于排查，而非确证
7. 重复故障历史 你基于保留的告警和遥测数据构建的查询 反复发出告警的节点 部分可以：它能找出值得及早检查的节点

第 1–3 层是唯一能够检测静默 SDC 的层，它们位于你的训练代码中。第 4 层将这些层的告警转换为实例 ID，HyperPod 各层则为告警提供佐证并完成闭环。

前提条件

要跟随本文操作，你需要：

  • 一个由 Amazon EKS 编排的 SageMaker HyperPod 集群，至少包含三个 GPU 节点。环形审计要对每项待判定的比较得出结论，需要三个不同的节点；权重比较则需要每个权重的三个副本，才能指出异常副本。请参阅使用 Amazon EKS 编排 SageMaker HyperPod 集群。
  • 一个 PyTorch DDP 训练作业，其中每个副本都执行自己的优化器步骤，并且数据流水线能够重建任意 rank 在指定训练步使用的微批次，例如使用带种子的采样器。
  • 存储在共享存储、Amazon FSx for Lustre 或 Amazon Simple Storage Service（Amazon S3）上的检查点。替换节点会销毁其根卷和辅助卷，包括本地 NVMe 上的所有内容。
  • 用于关联分析步骤的 SageMaker HyperPod 可观测性附加组件。如果需要 ECC、NVLink 和限速计数器，请启用高级 DCGM 指标。
  • 通过 kubectl 访问集群的权限，以及执行 sagemaker:StartClusterHealthCheck 和 sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes 所需的 AWS Identity and Access Management（IAM）权限。请参阅手动隔离、替换或重启节点。

步骤 1：在训练循环中通过三项检查进行检测

数据并行会同时训练模型的多个拷贝，称为副本。每个副本使用批次中不同的数据切片进行训练。每次反向传播后，all-reduce 对各副本的梯度求平均，每个副本在 optimizer.step() 中应用相同的平均值。下面展示三个副本中的同一个权重，学习率为 0.1：

副本 0 副本 1 副本 2
初始权重 0.500 0.500 0.500 相同
本地梯度 0.20 0.40 0.30 不同（数据不同）
平均梯度 0.30 0.30 0.30 all-reduce 后相同
训练步后的权重 0.470 0.470 0.470 相同

本地梯度各不相同，因为每个副本看到的数据不同。而在优化器步骤之后，权重必须逐位完全相同。

故障发生的位置决定了哪项检查能够发现它。如果副本 1 算出的本地梯度是 4.00，而不是 0.40，all-reduce 会将该错误传播到每个副本：三个副本都应用同一个错误更新，而它们的权重仍然一致。只有副本 1 的本地梯度显得不同，而且只在 all-reduce 之前如此。如果副本 1 在优化器步骤期间或之后损坏了某个权重，其权重就不再与其他副本一致。有一个例外：某个副本权重中的 NaN 或 Inf 会通过下一次 all-reduce 传播到每个副本，之后各副本又会一致。all-reduce 内部的故障，例如某块 GPU 错误地累加了部分和，也会以相同方式影响每个副本。

因此，计算路径故障必须在优化器步骤之前、错误梯度仍可被丢弃时捕获；更新过程中或已存储权重中的故障则必须在之后捕获。有限的错误值需要通过重新计算来检测：比较各副本的梯度范数只能捕获 NaN 和 Inf（请参阅为什么不比较本地梯度范数？）。由此，每个 DP rank 都需要在每个训练步中按固定顺序执行三项检查：

  1. 非有限梯度检查 – 在 all-reduce 之前，标记本地梯度为 NaN 或 Inf 的任何 rank。这会在 GPU 的前向或反向传播出现数值爆炸的当步捕获它，并指出对应 GPU。在 all-reduce 之后、更新之前，也检查归约后的梯度是否存在 NaN 或 Inf。
  2. 环形重放审计 – 在审计步的优化器步骤之前，每个 rank 都重新计算另一个节点上某个 rank 的微批次。它逐位比较损失值，并在使用确定性内核时比较每个参数的梯度指纹。这可以捕获计算路径中的有限错误值。
  3. 权重指纹比较 – 在优化器步骤之后，每隔 N 步以及每次保存检查点之前，比较每个副本的权重指纹。这可以捕获优化器步骤中以及已存储权重中的故障。

本步骤中的代码适用于 PyTorch DDP。有关张量并行、流水线并行或上下文并行，请参阅DDP 之外。

执行顺序

为什么不比较本地梯度范数？

一种直观的初始设计，也是我们最初采用的设计，是标记本地梯度范数偏离该步中位数超过 k 个中位数绝对偏差（MAD）的 rank。我们在 32 块 H100 上训练一个 9.53 亿参数模型，记录了 4 个实例上三次无故障运行中每个训练步、每个 rank 的本地梯度范数（共 22,800 步，见无故障运行），结果表明这种检验无效：

  • 正常情况下的分布范围太宽 – 每个 rank 看到的数据不同，因此正常本地范数在前 800 步中就已经达到 224 MAD，在全部正常训练步中则达到 1,240 MAD。
  • 低误报阈值看不到任何有限错误 – 当 k = 336，即前 800 个正常训练步中最高得分的 1.5 倍时，它在剩余 22,000 个正常训练步中产生了 11 次误报。而有限值故障的得分远未接近这个阈值：即使将一个激活值乘以 10,000，故障 rank 的得分也从未超过 6.9。

通过指纹比较

检查 2 和检查 3 比较不同 GPU 上的张量。传输完整张量的成本过高，因此将每个张量缩减为一个指纹：对原始位模式计算两个 64 位和，一个为普通求和，另一个按位置加权。对于元素数少于 2³²、每个元素最多 4 字节的张量，改变其中一个或两个元素必然会改变指纹。这涵盖了我们注入的所有权重故障。更大范围的变化原则上可能相互抵消，因此指纹相同是张量相同的有力证据，但不是证明。位置加权和很重要：在我们的测试中，交换两个权重值，以及对两个值进行相互补偿的修改，都没有改变普通和，只有加权和捕获了它们。

_INT_VIEW = {1: torch.uint8, 2: torch.int16, 4: torch.int32, 8: torch.int64}

@torch.no_grad()
def fingerprints(tensors, chunk=1 << 24):
    # ... picks the device and allocates out: one row of two int64 per tensor
    for k, t in enumerate(tensors):
        if t is None:
            continue
        bits = t.detach().contiguous().view(-1).view(_INT_VIEW[t.element_size()])
        for i in range(0, bits.numel(), chunk):  # chunked to bound temporary memory
            b = bits[i:i + chunk].to(torch.int64)
            pos = torch.arange(i + 1, i + 1 + b.numel(), dtype=torch.int64, device=dev)
            out[k, 0] += b.sum()
            out[k, 1] += (b * pos).sum()
    return out

检查 1：all-reduce 前后的 NaN/Inf 梯度

一个 DDP 通信钩子在求平均之前记录每个 rank 的本地梯度。它存储每个梯度桶的范数平方，并在确定性审计步中存储每个参数的梯度指纹（供检查 2 使用）。然后，它将梯度桶传递给 PyTorch 的标准 all-reduce。

反向传播后，nonfinite_ranks 从每个 rank 收集一个标量，并返回本地梯度范数为 NaN 或 Inf 的 rank。第一个被标记的 rank 就是故障 rank。如果应用了该训练步，NaN 会在下一步传播到每个 rank。

def local_stats_hook(stats, bucket):
    stats.sq.append(bucket.buffer().float().pow(2).sum())
    if stats.record_fingerprints:  # per parameter, before allreduce_hook divides in place
        rows = [stats.row[p.data_ptr()] for p in bucket.parameters()]
        stats.fp[rows] = fingerprints(bucket.gradients())
    return allreduce_hook(stats.dp_group, bucket)

def attach(ddp_model, dp_group):
    stats = LocalStats(dp_group, list(ddp_model.module.parameters()))
    ddp_model.register_comm_hook(state=stats, hook=local_stats_hook)
    return stats

def nonfinite_ranks(stats):
    """After backward: global ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf."""
    local = torch.stack(stats.sq).sum().sqrt().reshape(1)
    n = dist.get_world_size(stats.dp_group)
    gathered = [torch.empty_like(local) for _ in range(n)]
    dist.all_gather(gathered, local, group=stats.dp_group)
    bad = ~torch.isfinite(torch.cat(gathered).cpu())
    return [dist.get_global_rank(stats.dp_group, r) for r in bad.nonzero().flatten().tolist()]

train() 还会检查 all-reduce 之后的梯度。在归约内部产生的 NaN 或 Inf 会以相同方式传播到每个副本，因此各副本仍然一致，检查 3 也会放行。如果没有这项检查，NaN 会使每个副本的权重都变成 NaN，而该步恰好需要保存的检查点会带着这些权重被保存，并标记为通过检查。clip_grad_norm_ 已经会计算归约后梯度的范数，因此这项检查每步只增加一次仅含一个元素的 all-reduce。归约中的有限值错误仍会通过所有检查。

如果使用 fp16 和梯度缩放器训练，请排除缩放器已经跳过的溢出步。bf16 没有这类溢出步。

检查 2：优化器步骤之前的环形重放

在 optimizer.step() 之前，每个副本都持有相同的权重。因此，在反向传播和优化器步骤之间，任意 rank 都可以重新计算其他任意 rank 的微批次，并且在使用确定性内核时，必须得到逐位相同的结果。

在审计步，每个 rank r 都会重新计算 rank r + 8 的微批次：向前偏移 8 个位置，在 p5 实例上就是相隔一个节点。它使用未封装的模块，因此不会执行任何 all-reduce，并在之后恢复梯度、模块缓冲区和随机数状态。无论有多少个 rank 执行重放，重放都会阻塞作业，因此审计每个 rank 与只审计一个 rank 所花的实际时间相同。

随后，每个 rank 都出现在两项比较中：由对等 rank 重放它自己的微批次，以及它为其他 rank 重放的微批次。

  • 两项比较均不匹配：该 rank 在两次计算中都出错，因此它就是故障源。
  • 只有一项不匹配：任一方都可能出错。confirm 会就地判定：目标之后第八个位置、位于第三个节点上的 GPU，以及目标自身，再次重放目标的微批次。这还能区分目标可以复现的持续性故障，以及目标无法复现的瞬态故障。
def ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats, local_loss, offset, with_grads):
    # ... g is the DP group, n its size, and me this rank's position in it
    target = dist.get_global_rank(g, (me + offset) % n)
    replay = _replay(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch(step, target), with_grads)
    # ... v = [this rank's own loss bits and gradient fingerprints, its replay of target]
    dist.all_gather_into_tensor(out, v, group=g)
    table = out.view(n, 2, -1).cpu()  # per DP rank: [own result, its replay of its target]
    pairs = [(dist.get_global_rank(g, (r + offset) % n), dist.get_global_rank(g, r))
             for r in range(n) if not torch.equal(table[(r + offset) % n, 0], table[r, 1])]
    return pairs, table

def localize(pairs):
    hits = Counter(r for p in pairs for r in p)
    culprits = sorted(r for r, c in hits.items() if c >= 2)
    ambiguous = [p for p in pairs if not set(p) & set(culprits)]
    return culprits, ambiguous

def confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, pair, table, stats, offset, with_grads):
    # ... the third GPU (target + offset) and the target replay the target's micro-batch again
    third_r, self_r = v.cpu()
    orig, peer = table[ti, 0], table[ri, 1]
    if torch.equal(third_r, orig):
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": replayer, "kind": "replayer computed wrong"}
    if torch.equal(third_r, peer):
        kind = ("persistent" if torch.equal(self_r, orig) else
                "transient" if torch.equal(self_r, third_r) else "unclear")
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": target, "kind": kind}
    return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": None, "kind": "unattributable"}

只有当这三块 GPU 位于三个不同节点上时，确认过程才具有独立性。check_topology 会在训练开始前，依据每个 Pod 的 NODE_NAME 为每一对验证这一点，否则报错。

选择审计模式：

  • 默认内核：仅比较损失值。这要求前向传播的损失值能够逐位复现，我们的测试满足这一要求：正常重放的损失值与原始损失值逐位相同。梯度无法用这种方式比较，因为注意力的默认反向传播并不具有确定性。该模式可以捕获改变损失值的前向传播故障。
  • 确定性内核（deterministic_audits=True）：整个审计步都使用确定性算法和 math 注意力内核运行。此时梯度指纹也会匹配，因此审计还能捕获仅发生在反向传播中的故障。没有确定性实现的算子会报错，而不是产生误报。在我们的模型上，一个确定性审计步的耗时为默认训练步的 2.4 倍。

绝不要仅在可疑 GPU 自身上重放它的计算。存在持续性缺陷的 GPU 可以复现自己的错误答案。

检查 3：优化器步骤之后的权重指纹

在 optimizer.step() 之后，每个副本的权重必须完全相同，因此无需调整容差。每个 rank 都为每个权重张量计算指纹，并收集所有 rank 的指纹。

只有当某个 rank 的张量副本与严格多数，即超过半数的副本不同时，才会指出该 rank。如果只有两个副本，或分歧中没有严格多数，比较会报告不一致，但不会指出任何 rank。

def find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group):
    local = fingerprints(params).flatten()
    # ... all-gathers every rank's fingerprints into table: [dp_size, num_tensors, 2]
    differs = (table != table[0]).any(dim=2).any(dim=0)
    if not differs.any():
        return {"diverged": False, "suspects": []}
    suspects = set()
    for k in differs.nonzero().flatten().tolist():
        copies = [tuple(row) for row in table[:, k].tolist()]
        value, count = Counter(copies).most_common(1)[0]
        if 2 * count <= n:
            return {"diverged": True, "suspects": None}  # no strict majority for tensor k
        suspects.update(r for r, c in enumerate(copies) if c != value)
    return {"diverged": True,
            "suspects": sorted(dist.get_global_rank(dp_group, r) for r in suspects)}

每隔 N 步以及每个检查点步都运行这项检查。它是唯一在更新之后运行的检查，因此也是唯一能够阻止从损坏副本写出检查点的检查。在我们的测试中，一个在某次更新后立即被损坏的权重，在下一个检查点步被捕获，保存操作没有发生。如果不强制检查，保存就会继续使用损坏副本，而环形审计直到五步后的下一次审计才发现问题。

在一个 9.53 亿参数模型上，每次检查耗时 31.1 ms：每 10 步运行一次时，其开销相当于单步耗时的 2%。

将检查加入训练循环

train 在每一步都按图 2 的顺序执行，并在第一个告警处停止。它会在前向传播之前决定当前步是否为审计步，因为确定性比较要求原始计算也具有确定性。检查 1 或检查 2 触发时，它会将梯度清零并返回，不进行裁剪或应用更新，因此错误梯度永远不会进入权重或优化器状态，并且确认所需的精确状态仍然保留。裁剪后，它会检查归约后的梯度是否为 NaN 或 Inf，如果是，则在更新前返回。只有没有任何检查触发时，它才会保存检查点。

def train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, save_checkpoint,
          sched, start_step=0):
    # ... setup, including check_topology(dp_group, sched.peer_offset)
    for step, batch in enumerate(batches, start_step):
        audit = step % sched.audit_every == 0  # 0. decide first
        det = audit and sched.deterministic_audits
        # ... resets the hook's per-step state
        with deterministic() if det else nullcontext():
            loss = compute_loss(ddp_model, batch)  # 1. forward, backward
            loss.backward()
        nonfinite = nonfinite_ranks(stats)  # 2. non-finite check
        pairs, table = [], None
        if audit or nonfinite:  # 3. ring replay
            pairs, table = ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats,
                                      loss, sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det)
        if nonfinite or pairs:  # 4. gate
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            culprits, ambiguous = localize(pairs)
            verdicts = [confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, p, table, stats,
                                sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det) for p in ambiguous]
            return {"step": step, "check": "compute", "nonfinite": nonfinite,
                    "mismatched_pairs": pairs, "culprits": culprits, "verdicts": verdicts,
                    "suspect_window": _window(last_audit, step, start_step),
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        if audit:
            last_audit = step
        grad_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, sched.max_grad_norm)
        bad = (~torch.isfinite(grad_norm)).to(torch.int32).reshape(1)  # reduced gradient
        dist.all_reduce(bad, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=dp_group)
        if bad.item():
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            return {"step": step, "check": "reduced gradient", "suspect_window": [step, step],
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        ckpt = step % sched.ckpt_every == 0
        if step % sched.check_every == 0 or (ckpt and sched.check_on_checkpoint):
            wc = find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group)  # 5. weight check
            if wc["diverged"]:
                return {"step": step, "check": "weights", "suspects": wc["suspects"],
                        "suspect_window": _window(last_weights, step, start_step),
                        "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
            last_weights = step
        if ckpt:  # 6. checkpoint
            save_checkpoint(step, tags={"last_audit_pass": last_audit,
                                        "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights})
    return None

告警的 suspect_window 是从此次触发检查上一次通过以来的训练步范围。如果某个故障自出现起每步都持续发生，那么它就是在这个范围内开始的。间歇性故障可能更早就已存在，而任何检查都无法发现的故障可能存在于任意检查点中，因此应将这些标签视为检查在该步通过的记录，而不是已保存状态无损坏的证明。

训练脚本按如下方式调用它：

# ... imports, and the model, optimizer, and dataset setup
import sdc_order as S

stats = S.attach(ddp_model, dp_group)  # registers the comm hook, once
sched = S.Schedule(audit_every=10, deterministic_audits=True, check_every=10,
                   ckpt_every=100, peer_offset=8)  # 8 = GPUs per node

def compute_loss(model, batch):  # used for training AND replay
    x, y = batch
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits = model(x)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.float().flatten(0, 1), y.flatten())

def rebuild_batch(step, rank):  # exactly the micro-batch `rank` trained on
    return dataset.micro_batch(step, rank)

# ... batches(start) yields this rank's micro-batches and sets the learning rate
alarm = S.train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches(start), compute_loss, rebuild_batch,
                save_checkpoint, sched, start_step=start)
if alarm is not None:
    report_sdc(alarm)  # metric + log line; Step 2 maps the rank to a node
    sys.exit(3)

重放依赖以下条件：

  • 精确的微批次：rebuild_batch(step, rank) 必须返回该 rank 训练时使用的完全相同的微批次，例如通过带种子的采样器实现。
  • 相同的损失函数：compute_loss 在训练和重放中必须是同一个函数，包括 autocast，并且其中的任何随机性，例如 dropout，都必须按训练步和 rank 设置种子。
  • 模型中不存在集合通信或影响输出的状态：确认重放只在两个 rank 上运行，即目标和第三块 GPU，因此如果模型在前向或反向传播中调用集合通信（例如 SyncBatchNorm），遇到含义不明确的告警时就会挂起。如果前向传播既读取又更新某个缓冲区，正常重放也会产生差异。
  • 确定性设置：在训练进程启动之前设置 CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8，并确保模型中的每个算子都有确定性实现。
  • 对等 rank 偏移量：按节点依次为 DP rank 编号，这样当 peer_offset 等于每个节点的 GPU 数量时，每个重放者都会位于另一个节点上。check_topology 会拒绝不满足此条件的布局。
  • 本文未测试的情况：未使用的参数、梯度累积、BatchNorm，以及带副作用的前向钩子。如果存在未使用的参数，请设置 deterministic_audits=False，这会只比较损失值。

audit_every 是权衡成本与稳健性的主要设置：

  • 检测延迟：如果持续性的有限值故障也会发生在审计运行的内核中，就会在 audit_every 步内被捕获。确定性审计运行确定性内核和 math 注意力内核，因此如果故障只发生在其他训练步使用的默认内核中，就永远不会被审计到。
  • 损坏的更新：在审计捕获故障之前，最多可能应用 audit_every − 1 次损坏的更新。它们位于告警的 suspect_window 内。
  • 一次性故障：如果有限值故障只发生在某个非审计步，并且不再复现，就完全无法捕获。

将 ckpt_every 设置为同时是 audit_every 和 check_every 倍数的值，使每个检查点步都在更新前接受审计，并在更新后进行指纹检查。

每 10 步使用默认内核审计一次 177.0 ms +12.5%
每 100 步进行一次确定性审计 173.3 ms +10.1%
每 100 步使用默认内核审计一次 169.3 ms +7.6%

每种调度的开销中，约 7 个百分点与审计无关，来自每步运行的梯度钩子和两项 NaN/Inf 检查，以及每 10 步运行一次的权重检查。生产环境一个合理的起点是每 100 步进行一次确定性审计，在这里其开销为 10%。它仍能在 100 步内捕获持续性故障，包括仅发生在反向传播中的故障，代价是最多需要回滚 99 次损坏的更新。如果需要更快检测，例如对新增算力进行老化测试期间，或观察某个可疑节点时，可以每 10 步审计一次。请在自己的模型上测量开销：确定性注意力使用 math 内核，其开销随序列长度的平方增长。

在无故障运行中，15,320 个审计步和 3,080 次权重检查均未产生告警，据此可将误报率的上限估计为约每 5,100 个审计步 1 次（置信度 95%）。

步骤 2：将可疑 rank 定位到节点

rank 是一个逻辑 ID。要采取行动，你需要知道实例和物理 GPU。在 HyperPod EKS 上，Kubernetes 节点名称是带有 hyperpod- 前缀的实例 ID。通过 Kubernetes downward API 将其传入 Pod：

env:
- name: NODE_NAME  # on HyperPod EKS, spec.nodeName is "hyperpod-<instance-id>"
  valueFrom:
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: spec.nodeName

在作业启动时，记录一张将每个 rank 映射到其节点、实例和 GPU UUID 的表：

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

node = os.environ["NODE_NAME"]  # "hyperpod-i-0123456789abcdef0"
instance_id = node.removeprefix("hyperpod-")  # "i-0123456789abcdef0", what the Replace API takes
gpu_uuid = "GPU-" + str(torch.cuda.get_device_properties(torch.cuda.current_device()).uuid)
info = {"rank": dist.get_rank(), "node": node,
        "instance_id": instance_id, "gpu_uuid": gpu_uuid}
table = [None] * dist.get_world_size()
dist.all_gather_object(table, info)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    print("rank_map", table)  # log at every job start

如果作业已经在未使用 downward API 的情况下运行，可以通过 kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}' 从外部将 Pod 映射到其节点。

步骤 3：遏制损坏并检查 GPU 指标

告警触发时，首先停止作业。然后，在调查期间将可疑节点标记为不可调度，防止新的工作分配到该节点：

kubectl cordon <node-name>  # marks the node unschedulable; existing pods keep running

然后打开 SageMaker HyperPod 可观测性附加组件中的 GPU 运行状况仪表板，筛选出可疑节点和 GPU，并查看告警触发时的情况。如果该 GPU 的可纠正 ECC 错误、PCIe 重放、限速或温度上升，就更有理由认为硬件存在故障。面板正常并不能排除节点故障：纯粹的 SDC 往往不会在硬件遥测中留下任何痕迹。

步骤 4：确认，然后替换节点

运行步骤 1 中的检查后，告警已经会指出可疑 GPU。如果你观察到损失值突增等症状却没有告警，或希望在替换任何硬件之前排除软件问题，请先从排查成本低的解释入手。大多数损失值突增都不是 SDC，在数据 bug 上追查 SDC 会浪费数天时间：

Loss anomaly / suspected corruption
- Reproduces with the same seed on DIFFERENT nodes? -> deterministic bug, not SDC
- Goes away, or follows one node, when you move the job? -> strong SDC candidate
- DP replicas that must be bitwise identical disagree? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's step replayed on another node gives different bits? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's pre-all-reduce gradient is NaN or Inf? -> SDC candidate (use the first step it fired)
- Fleet-wide and gradual? -> likely recipe or optimizer
- Started at a data, config, or library change? -> usually software, but not proof

区分 SDC 与软件问题的检验标准，是问题是否跟随硬件出现：

  • 故障可复现并不能排除 SDC – Meta 将一个出错的工作负载固定到某个核心上，对特定输入每次都得到相同的错误答案。
  • 故障始于软件变更同样不能排除 SDC – Google 追溯的一起事件源于一次正确的库更新，该更新开始在有缺陷的核心上使用很少用到的指令。
  • 不要指望全局损失值能指向故障位置 – 前向故障首先改变故障 rank 自身的损失值，随后 all-reduce 将其梯度传播到每个副本。逐 rank 检查和重放才能提供位置信息。

判定告警的含义

告警 含义 建议操作
check == "weights"、suspects == [r] 更新后，rank r 的副本与严格多数副本不同 保持 r 所在节点不可调度。审核后替换
check == "weights"、suspects is None 副本之间不一致，但不存在严格多数 含义不明确：保持涉及的节点不可调度。检查 DCGM 并运行深度运行状况检查
culprits == [r] r 的两项环形比较均不匹配。这假定在相互重放的 GPU（本地索引相同的 GPU）中，最多只有一块故障 GPU。如果有两块，就可能指出一块正常 GPU 保持不可调度。审核后或故障再次发生后替换
判定为持续性故障 目标复现了自己的错误答案，第三块 GPU 的结果与重放者一致 保持不可调度。审核后替换
判定为瞬态故障 目标重试得到正确结果，并与第三块 GPU 一致。间歇性故障也可能表现相同 保持不可调度，直到以该节点为目标的审计或深度运行状况检查通过。如果再次发生，则替换
判定为重放者计算错误 出错的是执行重放的 GPU，而非目标 GPU 将重放者视为可疑对象，并再次确认
nonfinite 集合非空，无不匹配的配对 反向传播中出现了损失值未体现的 NaN 或 Inf，或梯度范数过大，超出了 float32 的范围（高于约 1.8 × 10¹⁹） 含义不明确：以可疑对象为目标进行审计，或检查 DCGM 并运行深度运行状况检查
check == "reduced gradient" 尽管每个 rank 的本地梯度都是有限值，all-reduce 后的梯度仍为 NaN 或 Inf。未指出任何 rank 含义不明确：保持作业停止，检查 DCGM，对作业中的每个节点运行深度运行状况检查，并从告警步之前保存的检查点恢复
判定为无法归因或不明确 三块 GPU 的结果无法相互印证 含义不明确：检查 DCGM，并对涉及的节点运行深度运行状况检查

在生产环境中，在你有证据证明这些检查在自身工作负载上的准确性之前，每次替换都应保留人工审批。像我们这样的合成测试无法确立这一点。

确认含义不明确的告警

深度运行状况检查是处理含义不明确告警的主要工具。其压力测试能捕获硬件会报告的故障，而细微的数据相关故障往往会通过检查。要对可疑实例组运行检查：

aws sagemaker start-cluster-health-check \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --deep-health-check-configurations '[{"InstanceGroupName":"<instance-group>","InstanceIds":["i-0123456789abcdef0"],"DeepHealthChecks":["InstanceStress"]}]'

替换节点

准备好替换节点后，你有两种选择。两者都会触发相同的 SageMaker HyperPod 恢复流程，详见手动隔离、替换或重启节点。

如果已启用自动节点恢复，可以为节点添加标签，让 SageMaker HyperPod 替换它，这种方式便于自动化：

kubectl label node <node-name> \
    sagemaker.amazonaws.com/node-health-status=UnschedulablePendingReplacement --overwrite

如果改用 API，请运行：

aws sagemaker batch-replace-cluster-nodes --cluster-name <cluster-name> --node-ids <instance-id>

在使用 Karpenter 自动扩缩容的集群上，BatchReplaceClusterNodes 会终止节点，但只有在待调度 Pod 需要节点时才会创建替代节点。替代节点加入后，训练作业会通过 SageMaker HyperPod 训练操作器或作业的重启策略重新启动，你的训练脚本则从告警的 suspect_window 起点之前保存的最新检查点恢复。加载检查点后、执行第一步之前，立即调用 find_divergent_ranks。替换会销毁节点的根卷和辅助卷，因此请将检查点存储在共享存储上。

自动化工作流

手动步骤用于帮助理解。在生产环境中，可用一个运行在你自己的集群和账户中的小型控制器来封装这些步骤：

  1. 触发： 训练作业以 Kubernetes 事件、小型自定义资源（例如 SDCReport{rank, job, step, check}），或基于 sdc_nonfinite_grad、sdc_replay_mismatch 和 sdc_divergent_tensors 等指标的 Amazon CloudWatch 告警来报告告警。
  2. 解析： 控制器通过 Kubernetes API 完成 rank → Pod → 节点的映射，然后去掉 hyperpod- 前缀，完成节点 → 实例 ID 的映射。
  3. 遏制： 将节点标记为不可调度。
  4. 决策： 按照步骤 4 中的表格处理。环形审计已经就地确认了含义不明确的配对，因此告警中包含判定结果。如果结果仍不明确，则对节点运行一次深度运行状况检查。
  5. 恢复： 如果需要替换，则请求人工批准，然后调用 BatchReplaceClusterNodes；如果启用了自动节点恢复，也可以设置节点运行状况标签。之后依靠训练操作器和你的检查点重载机制恢复，并将每个步骤记录到 CloudWatch。

可以将其构建为轻量级 Kubernetes 操作器，或构建为针对 CloudWatch 告警的 Amazon EventBridge 规则，由该规则调用 AWS Lambda 函数。

用例：在 SageMaker HyperPod 上测试这些检查

我们在一个由 Amazon EKS 编排的 SageMaker HyperPod 集群上进行了两轮测试，先使用 4 个、再使用 3 个 ml.p5.48xlarge 实例，每个实例配备 8 块 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPU，并使用 AWS Deep Learning Containers 训练镜像中的 PyTorch 2.9.0（CUDA 13.0）。模型是一个 9.53 亿参数的 Llama 风格解码器，包含 16 层，隐藏层维度为 2,048，有 16 个注意力头、32,000 个词元的词表，序列长度为 2,048 个词元。每块 GPU 每步处理 2 条序列（32 块 GPU 每步处理 131,072 个词元），权重、梯度和优化器状态使用 fp32，计算使用 bf16 autocast。我们使用 AdamW 训练，在 100 步线性预热后，学习率为 3 × 10⁻⁴，betas 为 (0.9, 0.95)，权重衰减为 0.1，梯度裁剪阈值为 1.0。数据是合成的：一个复制任务，词元服从 Zipf 分布，前半段会重复，并按 rank 和训练步设置种子，以便重建任意微批次。

故障场景

故障在选定的 rank 和训练步中注入到一个层里，即 16 个解码器块中第八个块的 MLP 下投影层：

  • 前向故障改变该层的输出，但保留其梯度路径，类似于前向传播中的一次错误乘法。
  • 仅反向故障改变该层输入或权重的梯度。
  • 权重故障在优化器步骤之后立即改变某块 GPU 上已存储权重的副本：位翻转、交换两个值，或对两个值进行相互补偿的修改。
  • 持续性故障会在故障 GPU 执行的所有计算中反复出现，包括它为其他 rank 执行的重放。瞬态故障只触发一次。

每个场景都从完成 400 个预热步后保存的快照重新开始，步数从该快照起计。除非另有说明，否则每 10 步使用确定性内核审计一次，每 10 步进行一次权重检查，每 20 步保存一次检查点。表格展示的是 4 个实例上的结果。在 3 个实例上，每个场景都在相同训练步、由相同检查触发相同告警，并指出相同的 rank。只有对等 rank 发生了变化。

DDP 之外

权重比较不限于 DDP。find_divergent_ranks 接受任意数据并行组，因此也适用于张量并行、流水线并行、上下文并行、HSDP 和混合专家，这些布局都保留每个权重的独立副本。它无法用于 ZeRO-1 或完整 FSDP 分片，在这些情况下，每个分片的更新只在一个 rank 上计算。本文仅使用 DDP 测试了这些检查和训练循环。

要在其他布局中使用它，请使用持有同一分片副本的组调用 find_divergent_ranks。如果只有两个副本，它能检测不一致，但无法指出哪个副本有故障。

如果你更希望由服务替你检查节点，SageMaker HyperPod 还提供 MultiNodeTraining 深度运行状况检查。它会在一批 GPU 节点上运行一个简短、固定的分布式训练作业，无需修改代码，并替换那些训练损失变成 NaN 或 Inf、发生发散或未能按时完成的节点。创建实例组时，可将其与 InstanceStress 和 InstanceConnectivity 一同选择，也可以使用 StartClusterHealthCheck 按需运行。它与本文的检查互为补充：在作业被分配到新节点或替代节点之前，用它筛查这些节点；再使用作业内检查，捕获你自身训练中那些始终未变成 NaN 或 Inf 的错误值。有关详情，请访问SageMaker HyperPod 深度运行状况检查。

清理

为避免持续产生费用，请删除为测试创建的资源。如果创建了 HyperPod 集群，请使用 aws sagemaker delete-cluster --cluster-name <cluster-name> 删除它。这只会移除 HyperPod 资源。在删除 HyperPod 集群后，请单独删除 EKS 集群、其附加组件以及所有 Amazon FSx 卷。请参阅删除 SageMaker HyperPod 集群。

结论

本文展示了如何检测数据并行训练中的静默数据损坏，以及如何将可疑节点交给 SageMaker HyperPod 替换。三项检查覆盖故障可能发生的三个位置：对每个 rank 的梯度和归约后的梯度执行 NaN/Inf 检查，通过环形重放将每块 GPU 的计算结果与另一个节点上的 GPU 进行比较，以及在更新后比较权重指纹。前两项应在优化器步骤之前运行，不应用未通过检查的训练步，并在每次保存检查点之前比较权重。SageMaker HyperPod EKS 集群上的节点名称可将可疑 rank 转换为实例 ID。然后隔离节点，回滚到可疑窗口之前的检查点，并让节点运行状况标签或 Replace API 完成恢复。

要开始使用，请查阅面向 Amazon EKS 的 SageMaker HyperPod 弹性功能，并试用配套仓库。要进一步了解，请参阅深度运行状况检查和可观测性附加组件。
